prompt.context_jp: 同じ頃、スタジアムの裏手では、家長__ひとり足早に人ごみを掻き分けていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 家長__ひとり足早に人ごみを掻き分けていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the correct particle. The narration is introducing Ienaga's action into the scene for the first time.

feedback.correct_en: The narrative is zooming into a new scene behind the stadium and introducing Ienaga as a newly spotted figure in that view — classic new-information が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark Ienaga as an already-established topic the sentence is commenting on, but here he is being newly presented to the reader at a different location.

contrast_examples.jp: 家長が人ごみを掻き分けていた。
contrast_examples.en: (There was) Ienaga, pushing through the crowd. (new sight)

contrast_examples.jp: 家長は人ごみを掻き分けていた。
contrast_examples.en: As for Ienaga, he was pushing through the crowd. (already in focus)

prompt.context_jp: こはぜ屋のテレビ前でも、息を潜める時間が続いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: あけみ__祈るように画面を見つめ、富島__無言で腕を組んでいる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits both blanks. Two already-known characters are contrasted doing different things.

feedback.correct_en: Both Akemi and Toshima are already in the scene; the sentence contrasts what each of them is doing. は naturally sets up this A-は..., B-は... parallel contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present each as newly spotted, but we already know who's in front of the TV — the point is comparing their reactions, not announcing them.

contrast_examples.jp: あけみは祈り、富島は黙っている。
contrast_examples.en: Akemi prays; Toshima stays silent. (contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: あけみが祈っている。
contrast_examples.en: (Look —) Akemi is praying. (newly noticed)

prompt.context_jp: 「心配いりませんよ ____フルマラソンなんですから」
prompt.prompt_jp: これ__フルマラソンなんですから。
prompt.prompt_en: The speaker is explaining the nature of the race to calm Akemi.

feedback.correct_en: 'これはフルマラソンなんです' sets 'this (race)' as the topic and explains what it is — a defining/explanatory statement. は is standard with 〜なんです explanations.
feedback.incorrect_en: 'これが' would single out 'this one' exhaustively ('THIS is the full marathon'), which doesn't match the reassuring, explanatory tone.

contrast_examples.jp: これはフルマラソンだ。
contrast_examples.en: This is a full marathon. (explaining what it is)

contrast_examples.jp: これがフルマラソンだ。
contrast_examples.en: THIS is the full marathon. (identifying/pointing out)

prompt.context_jp: 「分かってる__ 茂木だけじゃないっすよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 分かってるの__茂木だけじゃないっすよ。
prompt.prompt_en: The speaker is pushing back: it isn't ONLY Mogi who understands the strategy.

feedback.correct_en: '〜のは〜だけじゃない' is a cleft that contrasts 'the one who understands' against the assumption that it's only Mogi. は sets up this contrastive frame.
feedback.incorrect_en: が here would signal exhaustive identification ('the one who understands IS X'), which doesn't fit the 'not only' pushback.

contrast_examples.jp: 来たのは彼だけじゃない。
contrast_examples.en: He isn't the only one who came. (contrastive cleft)

contrast_examples.jp: 来たのが彼だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who came is him. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 「さあ そして 茂木です ダイワ食品の 茂木__前に出てきました」
prompt.prompt_jp: ダイワ食品の 茂木__前に出てきました。
prompt.prompt_en: A live race commentator is reporting a sudden visible move.

feedback.correct_en: Live sports commentary describing a new event unfolding right now almost always takes が — it reports the action as a fresh observation.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn Mogi into a general topic ('as for Mogi, he moved forward'), losing the breaking-news feel of the broadcast.

contrast_examples.jp: 茂木が前に出てきました！
contrast_examples.en: Mogi has come forward! (live report)

contrast_examples.jp: 茂木は前に出てきました。
contrast_examples.en: Mogi, (as topic), came forward. (reflection)

prompt.context_jp: レースはいよいよ勝負どころに差し掛かる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 茂木のペース配分__決して極端ではなく、むしろ中庸を心得た走りだった。
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator is describing Mogi's pacing as a general trait.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence takes Mogi's pacing as the topic and makes a general characterization about it. は is the natural choice for this descriptive 'as for X, it is Y' pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the pacing as newly observed information, but here it's being commented on, not introduced.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のやり方は極端ではない。
contrast_examples.en: His approach isn't extreme. (characterization)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のやり方が極端だ。
contrast_examples.en: (It's) his approach (that) is extreme. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 「ここで ケニアの サイラス･ジュイ__抜け出しました」
prompt.prompt_jp: ここで ケニアの サイラス･ジュイ__抜け出しました。
prompt.prompt_en: The commentator announces a breakaway move in the race.

feedback.correct_en: A sudden race event — someone breaking from the pack — is reported with が. The focus is on 'who did it,' presented as fresh news.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make Jui an already-established topic and sound more like a recap than a live call.

contrast_examples.jp: ジュイが抜け出した！
contrast_examples.en: Jui has broken away! (live report)

contrast_examples.jp: ジュイは抜け出した。
contrast_examples.en: As for Jui, he broke away. (narrative recap)

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢__無意識にテレビへ詰め寄っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢__無意識にテレビへ詰め寄っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator returns to Miyazawa, an already-known main character, and comments on what he was doing.

feedback.correct_en: Miyazawa is the central established figure; the narrator is picking him up again as topic and describing his unconscious action. は fits the 'as for Miyazawa' flow.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would frame his approach to the TV as a surprising new sight, but the surrounding narration is reflective and continues his already-ongoing emotional state.

contrast_examples.jp: 宮沢は画面に見入っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Miyazawa (topic) was glued to the screen.

contrast_examples.jp: 宮沢が画面に見入っていた。
contrast_examples.en: There was Miyazawa, glued to the screen. (newly noticed)

prompt.context_jp: カーブを曲がったところで、画面が思わぬ光景を映し出した。
prompt.prompt_jp: 誰か__路面に倒れ込んでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: A shocking new image appears on screen.

feedback.correct_en: '誰か' (someone) is indefinite and newly introduced — classic が territory. The sentence reports a sudden, newly-perceived sight.
feedback.incorrect_en: '誰かは' is almost ungrammatical here; a nonspecific 'someone' can't be an established topic without further context.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰かが倒れている。
contrast_examples.en: Someone is lying collapsed. (new sight)

contrast_examples.jp: その人は倒れていた。
contrast_examples.en: That person had collapsed. (already known)

prompt.context_jp: 「ここまで来たら もう 駆け引きどころじゃない 気持ちの強いほう__勝つ！」
prompt.prompt_jp: 気持ちの強いほう__勝つ！
prompt.prompt_en: A principle: the one with the stronger will wins.

feedback.correct_en: This is an exhaustive-identification が: among the possibilities, it is specifically the mentally stronger one that wins. The structure 〜ほうが〜 picks out the winning side.
feedback.incorrect_en: '気持ちの強いほうは勝つ' would read as a general topic comment and sound oddly flat; the point is to single out which side prevails.

contrast_examples.jp: 速いほうが勝つ。
contrast_examples.en: The faster one is the one that wins.

contrast_examples.jp: 速いほうは勝つ。
contrast_examples.en: (Awkward) As for the faster one, it wins.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢の顔から、血の気__引いた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢の顔から、血の気__引いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Describing an involuntary physical reaction.

feedback.correct_en: '血の気が引く' is a fixed collocation meaning 'to go pale.' Idiomatic body-reaction expressions use が for the subject of the sudden change.
feedback.incorrect_en: '血の気は引いた' sounds unnatural; the phrase is lexicalized with が and reports a newly-occurring physiological event.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔から血の気が引いた。
contrast_examples.en: The color drained from his face.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は青ざめた。
contrast_examples.en: He turned pale. (different phrasing)

prompt.context_jp: ゴールテープ__胸に触れた瞬間、時が一気に音を取り戻した。
prompt.prompt_jp: ゴールテープ__胸に触れた瞬間、時が一気に音を取り戻した。
prompt.prompt_en: The climactic moment the finish-line tape touches the runner's chest.

feedback.correct_en: Inside the 〜瞬間 subordinate clause, the subject takes が — subordinate clauses describing a specific event prefer が over は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside a 〜瞬間/〜時 clause would awkwardly impose a topic reading on an embedded event description.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が来た瞬間、拍手が起きた。
contrast_examples.en: The moment he came, applause broke out.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は来た。瞬間、拍手が起きた。
contrast_examples.en: (Breaks the single clause — unnatural fusion.)

prompt.context_jp: 「今 僕__ここに立てているの__ 僕だけの力ではありません」
prompt.prompt_jp: 僕がここに立てているの__僕だけの力ではありません。
prompt.prompt_en: Mogi's humble victory speech: 'The reason I can stand here is not thanks to my own strength alone.'

feedback.correct_en: '〜のは〜ではない' is a cleft construction. は marks the nominalized clause as the topic being qualified. Inside the clause, 僕が is new-info が; the outer frame takes は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が outside the cleft would double up two 'が's and break the 'as for the fact that..., it's not...' topic-comment structure.

contrast_examples.jp: ここに立てているのは皆のおかげだ。
contrast_examples.en: The fact that I can stand here is thanks to everyone.

contrast_examples.jp: ここに立てているのが僕だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one standing here is me. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: インタビューが放送されたその日から、こはぜ屋の電話__鳴り止まなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: こはぜ屋の電話__鳴り止まなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: A general ongoing situation about the shop's phone after the broadcast.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence states a durative characterization of Kohaze-ya's phone after the broadcast — a topic comment. は fits this 'about X, Y was going on' description.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight the phone as a newly introduced subject, but it's being commented on against the already-established story context.

contrast_examples.jp: 店の電話は鳴り止まなかった。
contrast_examples.en: The shop's phone wouldn't stop ringing. (characterizing)

contrast_examples.jp: 電話が鳴った。
contrast_examples.en: The phone rang. (single new event)

prompt.context_jp: 「オン ユア マーク」
prompt.prompt_jp: 号砲__響き、選手たちが飛び出していく。
prompt.prompt_en: The starting gun fires, kicking off the race.

feedback.correct_en: A single, sudden event ('the gun went off') with an indefinite subject takes が. This is textbook event-reporting が.
feedback.incorrect_en: '号砲は響き' would require the starting gun to already be a topic under discussion, which it isn't — it's the triggering event itself.

contrast_examples.jp: ベルが鳴った。
contrast_examples.en: The bell rang. (event)

contrast_examples.jp: そのベルは学校の合図だ。
contrast_examples.en: That bell is the school's signal. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: こはぜ屋が一足一足重ねてきた試作の日々が、この一瞬に凝縮されていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ____も積もれば山となるという言葉の通り、こはぜ屋が一足一足重ねてきた試作の日々が、この一瞬に凝縮されていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the proverb: 'Even ___, piled up, becomes a mountain.'

feedback.correct_en: The set proverb is 塵も積もれば山となる — 'even dust piles up into a mountain.' It's the standard idiom in Japanese for small efforts adding up.
feedback.incorrect_en: 砂 (sand) and 灰 (ash) sound plausible but are not the fixed form; swapping them produces a non-idiom native speakers won't recognize.

contrast_examples.jp: 塵も積もれば山となる。
contrast_examples.en: Many a little makes a mickle. (set proverb)

contrast_examples.jp: 小さな努力の積み重ねが大事だ。
contrast_examples.en: Accumulating small efforts matters. (paraphrase)

prompt.context_jp: 「あいつらは ____勘定 抜きで 命 削って走ってんだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: あいつらは____勘定抜きで命削って走ってんだ。
prompt.prompt_en: They run with their lives on the line, setting aside what?

feedback.correct_en: 損得勘定 ('calculation of gain and loss') is a fixed compound. Here Ienaga is saying the runners act without weighing profit versus loss.
feedback.incorrect_en: 勝負勘定 and 計算勘定 aren't established collocations; only 損得 pairs idiomatically with 勘定 in this sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 損得勘定抜きで動く。
contrast_examples.en: To act without calculating gain and loss.

contrast_examples.jp: 損得を考えずに行動する。
contrast_examples.en: To act without thinking of profit. (paraphrase)

prompt.context_jp: いっぽうで茂木は、依然として静かに____を窺っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 茂木は依然として静かに____を窺っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Mogi was quietly watching for his opportunity.

feedback.correct_en: 機を窺う ('to watch for one's chance') is a set collocation. 機 here means opportunity/moment, and it pairs specifically with 窺う.
feedback.incorrect_en: 時を窺う and 場を窺う aren't idiomatic. 時機を見る or 様子を窺う exist, but with 窺う and this meaning, 機 is the established partner.

contrast_examples.jp: 機を窺う。
contrast_examples.en: To watch for one's chance.

contrast_examples.jp: 様子を窺う。
contrast_examples.en: To observe the situation.

prompt.context_jp: 倒れた選手のもとに歩み寄り、そっと手を____。
prompt.prompt_jp: そっと手を____。
prompt.prompt_en: Mogi gently extends his hand to the fallen runner.

feedback.correct_en: 手を差し伸べる means 'to extend a helping hand' — the standard set phrase for offering compassion or aid.
feedback.incorrect_en: 引き寄せる means to pull toward oneself; 振り払う means to shake off. Both carry opposite nuances to the kindness shown here.

contrast_examples.jp: 困った人に手を差し伸べる。
contrast_examples.en: To extend a hand to someone in trouble.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の手を振り払った。
contrast_examples.en: He shook off the other's hand. (rejection)

prompt.context_jp: 「あんな姿を____にしたら どうしても 余計な力が入って ペースが乱れてしまう」
prompt.prompt_jp: あんな姿を____にしたら、余計な力が入ってしまう。
prompt.prompt_en: 'When one sees that sight with one's own eyes...'

feedback.correct_en: 目の当たりにする is a set expression meaning 'to witness directly / with one's own eyes.' The fixed phrase takes 目の当たり + にする.
feedback.incorrect_en: 目の前にする exists but means 'to have (something) in front of one'; it lacks the 'witness something striking firsthand' nuance. 耳の端 isn't idiomatic here.

contrast_examples.jp: 惨状を目の当たりにする。
contrast_examples.en: To witness a terrible scene firsthand.

contrast_examples.jp: 試験を目の前にする。
contrast_examples.en: To have the exam right before one. (temporal)

prompt.context_jp: 長年、法律を自分には関係ないと思うような振る舞いを続けてきた男に、ようやく____の崩れる音が聞こえていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ようやく____の崩れる音が聞こえていた。
prompt.prompt_en: The sound of his own foundation crumbling beneath him.

feedback.correct_en: 足元が崩れる ('the ground beneath one crumbles') is the standard metaphor in Japanese for one's footing or position collapsing. 足元 = one's feet/footing.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手元 (at hand) and 胸元 (chest area) don't form this collapse metaphor. Only 足元 carries the sense of the ground supporting you giving way.

contrast_examples.jp: 足元が崩れる。
contrast_examples.en: One's footing collapses.

contrast_examples.jp: 手元が狂う。
contrast_examples.en: One's hand slips / one's aim falters.

prompt.context_jp: かつて誰にも見向きされなかった小さな足袋屋の靴が、いまや日常のなかに____つつあった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 小さな足袋屋の靴が、いまや日常のなかに____つつあった。
prompt.prompt_en: The small shop's shoes were gradually blending into everyday life.

feedback.correct_en: 〜に溶け込む ('to blend into') is the natural verb for something becoming a seamless part of daily life or society.
feedback.incorrect_en: 入り込む suggests intruding or working one's way in; 飛び込む is to dive/plunge in. Neither captures the gradual, natural blending nuance.

contrast_examples.jp: 社会に溶け込む。
contrast_examples.en: To blend into society.

contrast_examples.jp: 敵陣に飛び込む。
contrast_examples.en: To plunge into enemy territory.

prompt.context_jp: ここに至るまでの失敗と犠牲は、思い出すだけでも____ないほどのものだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 思い出すだけでも目も____ないほどのものだった。
prompt.prompt_en: The failures were so painful that even remembering them was unbearable to look at.

feedback.correct_en: 目も当てられない is a set phrase meaning 'too awful to look at.' The fixed verb inside is 当てる.
feedback.incorrect_en: 見られない / 開けられない look superficially plausible but the idiom uses 当てる specifically; swapping breaks the fixed form.

contrast_examples.jp: 目も当てられない惨状。
contrast_examples.en: A sight too wretched to behold.

contrast_examples.jp: 見るに堪えない。
contrast_examples.en: Unbearable to watch. (near-synonym)

prompt.context_jp: Miyazawa feels his own heart racing as if from a distance.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural for the narration?

choices.text: 宮沢は自分の胸が高鳴るのを、遠くの出来事のように感じていた。
宮沢が自分の胸は高鳴るのを、遠くの出来事のように感じていた。

feedback.correct_en: A natural 'double-subject' pattern: 宮沢は (topic) ... 胸が (embedded subject). The outer human experiencer takes は; the inner body-part subject takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: Flipping the particles turns Miyazawa into fresh news and his chest into an abstract topic — the result sounds backwards and unnatural.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は頭が痛い。
contrast_examples.en: He has a headache. (topic + inner subject)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が頭は痛い。
contrast_examples.en: (Unnatural swap)

prompt.context_jp: Miyazawa is shouting encouragement, no time left for strategy.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing better captures the heated moment?

choices.text: ここまで来たら もう 駆け引きどころじゃない。
ここまで来てしまったので 駆け引きの状況ではございません。

feedback.correct_en: 〜どころじゃない is a punchy spoken expression meaning 'no time for ~.' It matches the shouting-at-the-TV register of this scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: The second version is overly polite and bookish; the heat of the moment calls for colloquial, blunt phrasing.

contrast_examples.jp: 勉強どころじゃない。
contrast_examples.en: This is no time for studying!

contrast_examples.jp: 勉強をしている状況ではございません。
contrast_examples.en: (Overly formal paraphrase)

prompt.context_jp: Mogi dedicates his victory to Kohaze-ya during the post-race interview.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural for a public victory dedication?

choices.text: 今日の優勝は、こはぜ屋の皆さんにささげたいと思います。
今日の優勝を、こはぜ屋の皆さんにあげたいと思います。

feedback.correct_en: 勝利/優勝をささげる ('to dedicate one's victory') is the standard, dignified collocation for athletes thanking supporters. 〜は marks the dedication's topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: あげる ('give') is far too casual and concrete for an abstract dedication; it clashes with the formal interview register.

contrast_examples.jp: この勝利を家族にささげます。
contrast_examples.en: I dedicate this victory to my family.

contrast_examples.jp: この勝利を家族にあげます。
contrast_examples.en: I'll give this victory to my family. (odd/casual)

prompt.context_jp: Miyazawa tells his son to go gain experience at Metro Electric that Kohaze-ya cannot provide.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds more natural in context?

choices.text: うちでは得られない知識や経験を蓄積してきてくれ。
うちでは得られない知識や経験を集めてきてくれ。

feedback.correct_en: 知識/経験を蓄積する ('to accumulate knowledge/experience') is the idiomatic collocation for building up expertise over time. It carries the gravity Miyazawa intends.
feedback.incorrect_en: 集める means 'to gather/collect' and sounds like gathering physical items. Native speakers specifically pair 蓄積 with knowledge and experience here.

contrast_examples.jp: 経験を蓄積する。
contrast_examples.en: To accumulate experience.

contrast_examples.jp: 切手を集める。
contrast_examples.en: To collect stamps.

prompt.context_jp: Oohashi marvels at Kohaze-ya's resilience after visiting the new factory.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural as a surprised, emotional remark?

choices.text: まったく… 本当に しぶとい人たちだな こはぜ屋さんは。
まったく… こはぜ屋さんは本当にしぶとい人たちだなと思う。

feedback.correct_en: The right-dislocated 'こはぜ屋さんは' at the end is a natural spoken afterthought that emphasizes the emotional punch of 'しぶとい人たちだな.'
feedback.incorrect_en: The second version is grammatical but reads as a bland reported thought; it loses the sighing, impressed delivery the scene calls for.

contrast_examples.jp: 本当にしぶといな、あの人たちは。
contrast_examples.en: They really are tough — those folks. (right-dislocation)

contrast_examples.jp: あの人たちは本当にしぶといと思う。
contrast_examples.en: I think those people are really tough. (flat)
